stops.title: The Choking Boy & Crossed Candles
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Prison of Sebaste to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Two warm glowing tapered candles crossed gently in a darkened stone prison chamber as a grateful mother cradles her rescued child.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Every February 3 in parishes around the world, priests hold two crossed blessed candles (from Candlemas the day before!) against each person’s throat, praying: "Through the intercession of St. Blaise, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat."
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Tradition adds that a grateful poor woman whose pig Blaise had rescued from a wolf sneaked two bright candles into his pitch-black dungeon cell—giving us the exact crossed-candle symbol used every February 3!
stops.saintQuote: May the Lord deliver you from every ailment of the throat and every other evil.

stops.title: Sveti Vlaho: Guardian of Dubrovnik
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Ragusa to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 971 AD – Present · Walled City on the Adriatic
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit terracotta rooftops and golden baroque Church of St. Blaise framed by turquoise Adriatic sea walls in Dubrovnik.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Statues of St. Blaise ("Sveti Vlaho") holding a miniature model of Dubrovnik guard every gate and rampart of the Old City, and Dubrovnik’s grand Feast of St. Blaise on February 3 is recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: For over a thousand years straight—without missing a single February 3—Dubrovnik has released white doves and carried banners along the Stradun in honor of St. Blaise.
stops.saintQuote: Stand watch over this city and keep its gates in peace.

stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Madurai & Marava Country to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit palm-lined red-earth Tamil village road at dusk with an oil lamp glowing beside a simple saffron-robed ascetic.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Across Tamil Nadu, St. John de Britto is still affectionately called "Arul Anandar"—honored as a pioneer of deep cultural respect and dialogue between the Gospel and Indian spirituality.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Unlike missionaries who served only one caste, Arul Anandar walked fearlessly into villages of marginalized communities as well as royal courts, baptizing thousands across southern Tamil Nadu.
stops.saintQuote: Become all things to all people, that by love some may know the grace of God.

stops.title: The Red Sands of Oriyur
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Oriyur (Marava Kingdom) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.imageCaption: Radiant golden-crimson coastal Tamil Nadu shrine standing amid swaying palmyra palms and warm terracotta sands.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: The grand Shrine of St. John de Britto at Oriyur draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims from across South India—famous for its distinctive red soil revered in memory of the "Red Martyr."
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When John de Britto’s elderly mother in Lisbon heard her son had been martyred in India, she did not put on black mourning clothes—she wore her brightest festive gown and attended a Te Deum of thanksgiving!
stops.saintQuote: I await death with impatience; it has always been the object of my dearest prayers.

Walking calmly to the sandy plain of Oriyur on February 4, 1693, he prayed for his executioners and bowed his head joyfully.
